books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: William Lloyd Garrison, The Liberator, January 1, 1831

stimulus.source_note: William Lloyd Garrison, The Liberator, January 1, 1831. Public domain.
stimulus.text: I will be as harsh as truth, and as uncompromising as justice. On this subject, I do not wish to think, or speak, or write, with moderation. . . . I am in earnest — I will not equivocate — I will not excuse — I will not retreat a single inch — AND I WILL BE HEARD.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: In 1831, a Southern enslaver reading these words would most likely have concluded that Garrison

options.text: spoke for the majority of Northerners.
options.misconception: Background from the books: abolitionism was a minority position in the North in 1850, and Garrison’s paper spoke for a vocal few, not the majority.

options.text: wanted the federal government to buy enslaved people and free them.
options.misconception: Garrison demands an end to slavery, not a compensated purchase; buying freedom is a gradual plan he rejects.

options.text: was willing to bargain over slavery’s future in new territories.
options.misconception: His words refuse every bargain; a man who will not retreat an inch is not offering a deal.

options.text: meant to attack slavery itself, with no middle ground offered.

rationales.A: Background from the books: abolitionism was a minority position in the North in 1850, and Garrison’s paper spoke for a vocal few, not the majority.
rationales.B: Garrison demands an end to slavery, not a compensated purchase; buying freedom is a gradual plan he rejects.
rationales.C: His words refuse every bargain; a man who will not retreat an inch is not offering a deal.
rationales.D: A reader in 1831 could see the attack is on slavery itself — Garrison offers no bargain, no delay, and no middle ground.
rationales.general:
1. Read the vow as a Southerner would: a Northern editor promising to be heard, without moderation.
2. Background from the books: abolitionists were few in the North, but their words traveled, and Southern readers heard a threat to slavery itself.
3. Weigh the options: majority support, purchase, and bargaining all soften the message Garrison refuses to soften.
Remember: judge a source by how its audience would hear it, not only by what its author meant.
